stories.topic: How Amul beat Polson by making its butter rancid on purpose
stories.summary: During World War One the British Army wanted huge amounts of butter. Polson, a British company that grew up in India, built the first milk supply chain out of Gujarat and sent butter by train to Bombay and on to the UK. After the war Polson turned to the Indian market and dominated butter into the 1960s and early 70s; Ajay ate it as a child. Then Kurien's cooperative movement in Gujarat, backed by Danish technical and financial aid, built Amul with chilling plants and refrigerated vans and sent clean, high-quality butter to Bombay. It flopped, because Bombay found it bland. On investigation, the cause was Polson's poor refrigeration: its butter always arrived slightly rancid after the train journey, and Bombay had learned to expect that taste. Scientists identified the chemicals that form when butter goes rancid and added them to Amul. Amul then took off and drove Polson out of business.
stories.insight: A wartime supply chain shaped a market for half a century, and what people called 'taste' was really a side effect of bad old refrigeration. A better product can lose until it reproduces the flaws customers have learned to expect.
stories.quote: And the tastes of the Bombay consumer had become programmed to expect butter to taste a little rancid.

stories.topic: The Churchill Cigar Assistant that outlived Churchill
stories.summary: In the 1980s a Tamil Nadu government department called the CCA asked for a bigger budget, saying its allocation had been stagnant for a long time. A curious bureaucrat traced its origins to World War Two. Churchill could no longer get his favourite Cuban cigars because supply lines were cut, and the world's second-best cigars came from a town in Tamil Nadu. With India still under British rule, a department was set up to supply them to him: the Churchill Cigar Assistant. The war ended, Churchill died and India became independent, yet the department survived for decades and finally asked for more money. Amit credits the story to a book by Bibek Debroy.
stories.insight: A supply chain created by a wartime shortage outlived its only customer by decades. Once a government body exists, it keeps justifying itself long after anyone remembers why it was created.
stories.quote: the person in it has the audacity to say we need more budget.

stories.topic: Apple made the iPod shuffle less random so it would feel random
stories.summary: Amit offered this as a counterpart to the Amul story. The early iPod shuffle played songs truly at random, and users complained when it served up six Bruce Springsteen songs in a row, insisting that couldn't be random. Apple responded by adding an algorithm that broke up such streaks, so the shuffle would appear random without actually being random. Ajay added the statistician's view: the runs test checks randomness by looking at how often streaks of different lengths occur, so data from the original iPod would have shown that Apple's shuffle wasn't random.
stories.insight: Like Bombay's rancid butter, this is a company bending reality to fit what customers expect. People don't understand randomness: true randomness produces streaks that feel rigged.
stories.quote: So how Apple dealt with this complaint was by introducing an algorithm which made it non-random

stories.topic: Hiroo Onoda kept fighting for 29 years after the war ended
stories.summary: Amit read the opening of Walter Lippmann's Public Opinion. In 1914, on an island reached by a mail steamer only once in sixty days, English, French and German residents went on living as friends for six weeks without knowing their countries were at war. Amit noted that the same thing happened when World War One ended, with soldiers still killing each other while leaders shook hands. It reminded him of Hiroo Onoda, a Japanese soldier posted to an island in the Philippines around 1944 with orders to defend it to the death. Nobody told him the war was over, and he went on defending it for twenty-nine years. Amit first heard the story in Dan Carlin's 'Supernova in the East'.
stories.insight: People act on the picture in their heads, not on the world outside. Without information, a person can spend decades fighting a war that has already ended, which shows both the cost of information gaps and the folly of nation states.
stories.quote: No one told him the war was over.

stories.topic: Weeping in the rain to Blueprint for Armageddon
stories.summary: Amit started Dan Carlin's World War One series on a run. When his one-hour workout ended he couldn't go back up to his apartment and stood downstairs, still listening. On another run it began to rain and he stayed outside. That day Carlin read out the letters a group of soldiers wrote to their wives and girlfriends the night before a battle in which they all died, not knowing it would be their last night. Amit wept in the rain.
stories.insight: There are no sound effects and no script, just one man thinking aloud, and it moved Amit more than almost anything. That convinced him a story told well needs nothing else, and that audio is the most primal and powerful medium.
stories.quote: And he read out these letters. And I was weeping in the rain.

stories.topic: The book that kept him in an Irani cafe until 9 pm
stories.summary: Ajay was at Strand Book Stall in Bombay, needing to head home to Bandra before rush hour got worse. He came across 'Seizing the Enigma' at random, read the first page or two and bought it. Outside, the opening had so gripped him that he wandered aimlessly for a while, gave up on going home, sat down in a local Irani cafe and read the whole book until 9 pm.
stories.insight: A great book can override every plan you had for the day. Amit's verdict: this is the good life.
stories.quote: the only one life I could imagine at that moment was to drop everything and sit in an Irani shop and finish the book.

stories.topic: The scholar who quit to 'stand by his country'
stories.summary: A good friend told Ajay about a scholar at a Western think tank in Moscow who resigned when the Ukraine war began because he wanted to stand by his country. Ajay didn't have the wit to disagree in the moment, but on the show he says loyalty to a country is not loyalty to its state. Amit offered the opposite example: a group of top Russian chess players who published a letter against Putin right after the invasion. Many of them can no longer enter Russia and now play for other countries, and Amit calls that real bravery and patriotism.
stories.insight: Patriotism and obedience to the state are different things, and sometimes loving your country means opposing its government.
stories.quote: Standing by your country is not standing by the state.

recommendations.item: How Many Friends Does One Person Need?
recommendations.creator: Robin Dunbar
recommendations.context: Came up when Amit asked Ajay how he thinks about friendship, and Ajay cited Dunbar's number.
recommendations.reason: Dunbar's finding that we are wired for about 150 relationships, in tiers of 5, 15, 50 and 150, supports Ajay's view that our few close bonds make or break a life and deserve deliberate effort.

recommendations.creator: W.E.H. Lecky
recommendations.context: Amit's detour from Dunbar's number to the idea of the expanding circle.
recommendations.reason: It is the source of the 'expanding circle', the idea that through history we extend moral consideration from family to tribe to nation and beyond. Amit uses it to explain past horrors like slavery and to worry that today's circles are shrinking.

recommendations.creator: Peter Singer
recommendations.context: Amit credited Singer with extending Lecky's circle to animals. He wasn't sure which Singer book makes the case; the show notes link this one.
recommendations.reason: Singer argues the circle should include animals. Amit thinks people two hundred years from now may judge us for eating animals the way we now judge Jefferson for keeping slaves.

recommendations.creator: Don Bluth
recommendations.context: Ajay quoted the fable told to the Russian mice in this film, that there are no cats in America and the streets are filled with cheese.
recommendations.reason: He used it to mock the idea of a lost golden age of plenty in India's past, and to argue that philosophies like Jainism arose despite scarcity, not because of abundance.

recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay's essay introducing the term 'third globalization', which he lays out in this episode.
recommendations.reason: It gives the full argument that globalization isn't dead: it now runs inside a club of well-behaved countries, enforced through economic statecraft.

recommendations.item: An Indian view on dollar domination
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked alongside Ajay's claim that no coalition of countries can realistically build a currency or payment system to rival the dollar and the euro.
recommendations.reason: Expands on why anger at the power of the advanced economies won't produce a workable alternative, and why India should simply play by the rules of the game.

recommendations.item: Cross-border activities in India need more freedom, not less
recommendations.creator: Pratik Datta and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked to Ajay's critique of Indian capital controls, under which, for example, only poultry farms and nanotechnology firms may borrow abroad.
recommendations.reason: Argues that the state's fine-grained control of cross-border capital curbs the natural freedoms of people and firms.

recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay credits globalization for India's software and services export revolution, and points to the post-COVID boom in 'other business services'.
recommendations.reason: Shows how telecom made services tradable and why remote work after COVID opened a new phase of globalization for India.

recommendations.item: When world leaders thought you shouldn't need passports or visas
recommendations.creator: Jo Adetunji
recommendations.context: Linked to Ajay's account of the first globalization, when people travelled without passports or visas until World War One.
recommendations.reason: Documents how recent and avoidable state control of human movement really is.

recommendations.item: How Amul became utterly butterly delicious and salty
recommendations.creator: Vikram Doctor
recommendations.context: The background reading for Ajay's Polson-versus-Amul story.
recommendations.reason: Tells the full history of how Amul's first, too-perfect butter flopped in Bombay before it won the market.

recommendations.creator: Lapham's Quarterly
recommendations.context: Linked to Amit's story about Apple making the iPod shuffle non-random.
recommendations.reason: Covers how a product had to be engineered to match people's faulty intuitions about randomness.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: A piece from Range Rover, Amit's poker column for the Economic Times, which he recalled during the randomness tangent.
recommendations.reason: Explains why poker players who lose several hands in a row as 80% favourites are wrong to call the game rigged: over a large enough sample, unlikely runs are bound to happen.

recommendations.creator: Econlib
recommendations.context: Linked to Amit's simplification of Ricardo's trade theory.
recommendations.reason: A clear explainer of why trade benefits both sides even when one is better at everything.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Linked to Amit's point that a tariff on Mozambican ball bearings, meant to protect a supplier in Pune, hurts consumers.
recommendations.reason: Argues that tariffs quietly transfer wealth from poor consumers at large to rich interest groups.

recommendations.item: The Incredible Insights of Bastiat and Hayek
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Episode 6 of Everything is Everything, which Amit cited while discussing tariffs.
recommendations.reason: That is where the hosts first laid out how tariffs redistribute wealth from the poor to the rich.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Episode 16, which Ajay referred back to ('as we discussed in the China episode').
recommendations.reason: Background on Xi Jinping's nationalism and China's economic troubles, the conditions that led the advanced economies to start excluding China.

recommendations.item: 'Stop the war.' 44 Top Russian Players Publish Open Letter To Putin
recommendations.creator: Sam Copeland
recommendations.context: Linked to Amit's example of Russian chess players who opposed the invasion of Ukraine.
recommendations.reason: Amit sees these players as the true patriots: they stood up for their country by opposing its state.

recommendations.item: A trade deficit with a babysitter
recommendations.creator: Tim Harford
recommendations.context: Amit's 'Bravo, Babysitters!' chapter, based on Harford's Financial Times column of December 2005.
recommendations.reason: Harford always pays his babysitter and she buys nothing from him, yet both are better off. It shows why worrying about bilateral trade deficits makes no sense.

recommendations.item: How I Reversed My Type 2 Diabetes
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Episode 9, mentioned when Amit turned down the 'ghee shakkar' blessing.
recommendations.reason: Explains why Amit treats ghee as a superfood and sugar as poison.

recommendations.creator: Walter Lippmann
recommendations.context: Amit's first recommendation. He held up the physical book and read from its first chapter, 'The World Outside and the Pictures in Our Heads'.
recommendations.reason: A masterpiece for understanding how the media shapes what we believe and what to watch out for. Over a century old, it hasn't been made obsolete by any technological change.

recommendations.creator: Dan Carlin
recommendations.context: Amit's second recommendation, which he called perhaps the greatest podcast of all time.
recommendations.reason: Just one man talking conversationally, with no script and no sound effects, and it taught Amit about history, humanity and the power of audio storytelling.

recommendations.creator: Dan Carlin
recommendations.context: The Hardcore History episode (part one) where Amit first heard of Hiroo Onoda.
recommendations.reason: It is the source of the story of the soldier who defended a Philippine island for 29 years because nobody told him the war was over.

recommendations.creator: Dan Carlin
recommendations.context: The Hardcore History series on World War One: six episodes of about five hours each.
recommendations.reason: It kept Amit outside his building after runs and made him weep in the rain. He says it taught him about resilience, character, tragedy and the folly of nation states.

recommendations.creator: David Kahn
recommendations.context: Ajay's recommendation, a book he picked up at random at Strand Book Stall.
recommendations.reason: Its first two pages gripped him so completely that he skipped his commute and read the whole book in an Irani cafe until 9 pm.

core_ideas.concept: Friendship is finite and deserves deliberate effort
core_ideas.explanation: Robin Dunbar observed that we are wired for about 150 relationships, roughly the size of a hunter-gatherer band, in tiers of about 5 very close people, then 15, 50 and 150. Ajay prioritises these few bonds because they make or break a life. He adds two points. Age is irrelevant to friendship: there are petty, power-hungry old people and wise young ones. And friendships have their moments: a time and state of mind clicks and may never recur. That is fine; be grateful for it rather than blaming anyone.
core_ideas.quote: no man walks in the same friendship twice.

core_ideas.concept: The expanding circle, and how it can shrink
core_ideas.explanation: Lecky's idea, which Amit loves: humans extend moral consideration to a circle that starts with family and widens to tribe, nation and beyond. Everyone outside the circle might as well be an animal, which explains horrors like slavery and the treatment of women. Peter Singer argues the circle should reach animals. Amit's worry is that the circle can also contract, and rising nationalism and identity politics are shrinking it. Ajay adds that Mahavir and Jainism emerged in a protein-starved, far-from-golden society. Amit sees this as an early 'globalization' of the mind, before people could physically connect.
core_ideas.quote: That our circles are shrinking and not expanding, and that worries me greatly.

core_ideas.explanation: Many of us grow up assuming the world will keep getting better. Ajay thinks technology and GDP probably will improve, but a society's overall progress is far more complex. Many countries have gone terribly wrong, and a child's state could well get worse even as their technology improves.
core_ideas.quote: So it's a very iffy thing, it's something to aspire for. We should dream of it, but we should not count on it.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay defines globalization by five cross-border flows: ideas, people, goods, services and capital. It measures how far these flows, arising from voluntary transactions, are not shaped by national borders. Two forces drive it up and down. One is the state, which bans books, issues passports, levies customs duties and imposes capital controls. The other is technology, such as container ships, air freight and telecom, which keeps shrinking the cost of distance.
core_ideas.quote: the term globalization refers to the extent to which these five things are not being shaped by a national border.

core_ideas.concept: The First Globalization: capital flows downhill
core_ideas.explanation: Steamships, the Suez Canal and the telegraph set off the first globalization. States stayed out of the way: people travelled without passports, capital moved freely, and a lawyer could go practise in London. The only constraint was technology. Capital flowed downhill: projects in the US, Argentina and India raised money in London, where returns on extra capital were low, and invested it where returns were high. Keynes described a world around 1912 in which goods from everywhere arrived at your doorstep.
core_ideas.quote: It's important to remember that in the first globalization, nation states were not in the game.

core_ideas.explanation: Nationalism destroyed the first globalization. World War One brought passports, naval blockades and submarine attacks on shipping. Nazi Germany, wanting to go after the Jews, imposed the world's first capital controls. After 1945 Keynes and Harry Dexter White built the Bretton Woods order of GATT, the World Bank and the IMF, choosing fixed exchange rates. Keynes intuitively understood that you can't manage the exchange rate and also keep capital flowing freely, a point later formalised in Nobel-winning work. So capital controls were part of the deal. As a result, the world trade-to-GDP ratio only returned to its 1913 level in 1982.
core_ideas.quote: So in a very fundamental way, We lost freedom from 1913 to 1982, or maybe even a bit beyond.

core_ideas.concept: The Second Globalization: the unconditional welcome
core_ideas.explanation: From about 1982 to 2016–17, container ships, wide-body aircraft, computers and telecom cut the cost of distance. Fixed exchange rates and capital controls were dismantled, and the EU restored visa-free movement. India's software and services boom came from plugging into this world. Everyone was let in without conditions, on the assumption that prosperity would liberalise them. Instead, Deng's China became more authoritarian and Gorbachev's Russia became Putin's Russia.
core_ideas.quote: China was told, you're welcome in this club, no matter who you are. Vladimir Putin kept murdering people in London, but you're welcome to globalization.

core_ideas.explanation: Ricardo showed that cross-border trade raises welfare even when one party is better at everything. What matters is a difference in the ratio of how much better each side is at two different things. Amit's version: even if he were better at both podcasting and economics, he would still do the podcasting and leave the economics to Ajay.
core_ideas.quote: there has got to be a difference in the ratio between how much better you are as compared to me in two different things.

core_ideas.concept: Freedom works unless there's a market failure
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's public-economics test is that state intervention is justified only when there is a market failure, such as asymmetric information, an externality or a public good. Buying ball bearings from Mozambique involves none of these, so blocking or taxing it harms welfare and GDP. Amit adds two points. A tariff redistributes from the poor consumers at large to rich interest groups. And voluntary trade is consent, a positive-sum game, while state coercion destroys the gains.
core_ideas.quote: when the state intervenes in the absence of a market failure It has an adverse impact on welfare.
And the trade-off your moral calculus is between the deaths of soldiers and civilians versus the career destruction for an AI researcher in China.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay coined this term. Many people read the new restrictions as 'globalization RIP', but Ajay disagrees. The advanced economies, which include Japan, Taiwan and South Korea, have made basic good behaviour a condition of entry, starting with not invading your neighbour. Rogue states such as Russia, China, Iran and North Korea face the toolkit; for everyone else, globalization is deepening. One sign is the post-COVID boom in Indian services exports, as companies realised remote workers could just as well be in India. Ajay also argues that no coalition can realistically build a currency or payment system to rival the dollar and the euro.
core_ideas.quote: So it's not true that globalization is dead, but that the perimeter has shrunk.

core_ideas.explanation: The state is the community that holds a monopoly of physical violence in a territory. The country is its people. Ajay repeatedly separates the wonderful Chinese people from the saber-rattling Chinese state. Amit's concern about the third globalization is that the roughly 15% of the world being shut out consists of ordinary people who happen to live under rogue regimes, not rogue people.
core_ideas.quote: there is always a difference between a country and a state. They're two different things.

core_ideas.concept: Trade deficits are a non-problem: the double thank-you moment
core_ideas.explanation: Countries don't trade; individuals and firms do. Every voluntary cross-border deal is a 'double thank-you moment' where both sides think they got a great deal. So a bilateral deficit, such as India's with China, is just the sum of millions of mutually beneficial transactions, like Tim Harford's one-way spending on his babysitter. Thinking at the level of nations instead of individuals is the core mistake.
core_ideas.quote: It is individuals, it is firms that do trade, not countries that do trade.

core_ideas.concept: Current account deficits mean capital is coming in
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's two points of economics geekery. First, count goods and services together, because a widget, a potato and a haircut are all things you sell. India's standard data counts goods only. Second, the goods-and-services balance equals the current account deficit, which by an accounting identity is matched by capital inflow funding investment above domestic savings. Ajay's high-growth dream for India borrows from the first globalization: let capital flow downhill from advanced economies, where it earns poor returns, at 10–20% of GDP a year.
core_ideas.quote: So when anybody complains about the current account deficit, I just fundamentally don't understand it.

core_ideas.concept: Bide your time: India as a status quo power
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay doesn't resent the limits that come with the third globalization. India has no wish to conquer Bangladesh, so rules like 'don't invade your neighbour' cost it nothing, and the club is an open invitation that India uses every day. Borrowing Deng Xiaoping's advice, he says India should spend the next hundred years becoming an advanced economy and democracy, and rethink the world order only then.
core_ideas.quote: And I will borrow a piece of advice from the great man Deng Xiaoping, which is bide your time.

core_ideas.explanation: People misread streaks as evidence of rigging, whether it is six Springsteen songs in a row or five lost poker hands as an 80% favourite. Given enough repetitions, improbable sequences are certain to occur, and statisticians test real randomness with tools like the runs test.
core_ideas.quote: given a long enough number of iterations, any unlikely thing will happen

core_ideas.concept: The world outside and the pictures in our heads
core_ideas.explanation: Lippmann's framing: we act on our mental picture of the world, which can lag reality badly. Examples are islanders who stayed friends for six weeks after their nations went to war, soldiers who kept killing after the armistice, and Hiroo Onoda's 29 years on guard. Amit sees this as the key to understanding how the media shapes us, and says no technological change has made it obsolete.
core_ideas.quote: For six strange weeks they acted as if they were friends. when in fact they were enemies.

core_ideas.concept: Audio is the most primal medium
core_ideas.explanation: Hardcore History convinced Amit that you need nothing but a story and a voice. Storytelling was humanity's first entertainment, before music, television or binge-watching, and audio still carries the most emotional power.
core_ideas.quote: Audio is the most powerful medium in the world.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay explains that Indian capital controls let only poultry farms and nanotechnology firms borrow abroad. Amit: 'So if you're a really small chicken, you have the best of both worlds, poultry farms and nano chicken.'

Amit's version of comparative advantage: 'I am a better podcaster than you. I am also a better economist than you. However, I do the podcasting and I let you do the economics because hey, I can't spend all my time doing economics.'
After Ajay explains that ASML's machines make chip tracks about ten silicon atoms wide, Amit asks what the sensual organic sound is called when these atoms brush against each other: 'ASMR by ASML.'

Ajay describes an Indian importer telling his girlfriend he got a great deal on Chinese goods, while the Chinese exporter tells her boyfriend she got a great price from India. Amit: 'Everyone has a good romantic life in your stories.'

Pleased by Ajay's words, Amit refuses to say the traditional blessing 'aapke muh mein ghee shakkar' because he reversed his diabetes (Episode 9). He keeps the ghee, 'a superfood', and drops the sugar: 'Avoid shakkar, it is poison.'
Amit's Churchill cigar timeline: 'World War II ended, Winston Churchill died, India gained independence, not in that order.'

After a run of tangents (cigars, butter, iPods, runs tests), Ajay admits they're playing antakshari with stories: one person tells a story and the next picks up its last syllable. Amit suggests a whole episode like that and begs: 'Gentle reader, kindly don't unsubscribe right now.'
Ajay on the optimism of the second globalization, when the West welcomed everyone unconditionally: 'We felt confident that as you become rich, you will inevitably stop beating your wife.'
Ajay on a worn-out word: 'By the time a word graduates into the airport books, you know, it surely stops making much sense.'
An American Tail: to debunk myths of a lost golden age, Ajay quotes the fable told to the mice in Russia: 'there are no cats in America and the streets are filled with cheese.'

Chintaman Deshmukh took part in the Bretton Woods negotiations. Amit adds that Keynes wanted him as the IMF's first managing director, but the Americans objected: 'What Indian fellow, what are you talking about?'
Ajay on why Nazi Germany introduced the world's first capital controls: 'Nazi is German for nationalist socialist,' and Hitler brought in the controls when he wanted to go after the Jews.

Amit compares future judgement of meat-eaters to how we view slavery: just as Jefferson kept slaves and thought it morally fine, people two hundred years from now may look back and say 'oh they ate animals.'
Bibek Debroy, credited by Amit as the source of the Churchill Cigar Assistant story.
